title: Responsive, Themed, and Animated CSS
summary: Make pages adapt to every screen and preference with media and container queries, fluid sizes, themes, web fonts, and smooth motion.
intro: The same page gets opened on a small phone on a train, on a laptop, and on a monitor as wide as a desk. Some people browse in dark mode, some turn off animations because motion makes them dizzy, and some use high-contrast colors to read at all. You can't ship a different site to each of them, so one set of files has to adapt. That's what **responsive** design means. This lesson covers how a page learns the size of the screen and changes its layout, sizes that grow smoothly between small and large, components that fit whatever space they're put in, light and dark themes, web fonts that load without hiding your text, and motion that stays smooth and respects people who'd rather not have it.

steps.title: The viewport and media queries
steps.body:
Before a page can adapt to a screen, it needs to know how big the screen is, in units that mean the same thing on every device. This part covers what the browser measures, and media queries, the CSS that changes a layout at the sizes you choose.

## The viewport

The lesson on how a browser draws a page defined the viewport as the part of the browser window that shows the page. On a laptop it's the window minus the tabs and the address bar, and on a phone it's nearly the whole screen. Its width is the one number most responsive CSS depends on.

Phones need one line in the HTML to report it honestly. Without it, a phone pretends to be about 980 pixels wide and shrinks the page to fit, so the text comes out tiny. That line is the viewport meta tag from the lesson on HTML documents, which every page's head holds:

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```

It means: make the viewport as wide as the device, at normal zoom. Leave it out, and none of the media queries below will work on a phone.

## CSS pixels and device pixels

A phone's screen might have over a thousand real dots across, yet the browser reports it as about 390 pixels wide. That's the CSS pixel from the lesson on the cascade at work: a `px` isn't one dot on the screen, but a unit of length, about the size of a dot on an old monitor, so that `16px` text is readable on every device. A screen with three real dots per CSS pixel draws each one with a little square of nine dots, which is why text looks so sharp on it. The number of dots per CSS pixel is the **device pixel ratio**: 1 on older monitors, 2 on most laptops, and 2 or 3 on phones. For layout you only think in CSS pixels, and the browser handles the rest. Pictures are the one exception, which is why the HTML lessons gave images several sizes to choose from.

## Media queries

A **media query** is a block of CSS rules that apply only when a condition about the screen is true:

```css
@media (width >= 48rem) {
  .page {
    grid-template-columns: 16rem 1fr;
  }
}
```

Inside the block, the rules apply when the viewport is at least 48rem wide. Below that width, the browser skips them. The `>=` form is the **range syntax**, and every current browser understands it. Older code writes the same condition as `(min-width: 48rem)`, and you'll see both.

Use `rem` or `em` in media queries, not `px`. In a media query, both mean the browser's default text size, which is 16px unless the reader made it bigger in their settings. Someone who set a larger default then gets the narrow layout sooner, which is exactly what their bigger text needs.

## Mobile first

The usual way to write responsive CSS is **mobile first**: the rules outside any media query are for the narrowest screens, and each media query adds to them for wider ones. A narrow screen gets the simplest layout, usually one column, and wider screens add columns and space. It's easier to add a column than to take one away, and a phone with a slow connection never has to work through rules it overrides.

The width where a media query starts is called a **breakpoint**. Pick breakpoints from your content, not from a list of devices. Make your browser window narrow, then widen it slowly. When the line length gets too long or a row looks stretched, that's where a breakpoint goes. There are thousands of screen sizes, and a layout that's fine at every width doesn't care which one it's on.

## Other things a media query can ask

Width is the most common question, but not the only one:

- `(hover: hover)` is true when the main pointer can hover, like a mouse, and false on a touch screen. Keep important things out of hover-only menus, since a phone can't hover.
- `(pointer: coarse)` is true for a finger, a good time to make buttons bigger.
- `(orientation: landscape)` is true when the viewport is wider than it is tall.
- `print` applies when the page is printed or saved as a PDF.

Later parts of this lesson use the media queries that ask about people's settings, like dark mode.

## Trying sizes in DevTools

You don't need a drawer of phones. In Chrome's DevTools, the **device toolbar** button (Command, Shift, and M on a Mac, Ctrl, Shift, and M elsewhere) shows the page at a phone's width, with a handle to drag the width and a list of common devices. Check real phones too before you ship, since a real hand and a real screen show things the toolbar can't.

examples.title: A layout that gains a sidebar on wider screens
examples.prompt: Mobile first: one column by default, then a sidebar beside the content from 48rem wide.
examples.explanation: The first rule is for every screen. A grid with no columns listed has one column, so on a phone the sidebar and the content stack, one above the other, in the order they come in the HTML. The media query adds to it on screens at least 48rem wide, 768 pixels at the default text size: a 16rem sidebar column, a flexible content column, and more space everywhere. Nothing in the first rule has to be undone, since the wider layout only adds. Resize the window across the breakpoint and the sidebar jumps up beside the content. Writing it the other way round, desktop first, would need a `width < 48rem` query that resets the columns back to one.

examples.title: A menu that only hovers where hovering works
examples.prompt: On a device with a mouse, the submenu opens on hover. On a touch screen it never relies on hover, and a button opens it instead.
examples.explanation: The submenu starts hidden. A class, `open`, shows it, and JavaScript adds that class when someone taps or clicks the menu's button, which the JavaScript lessons teach. The hover rule sits inside `@media (hover: hover)`, so it only applies where the main pointer can hover. On a phone, the query is false and the submenu never depends on a hover the finger can't do. On a laptop, both work: hovering opens it, and so does clicking. Hover-only menus are a classic bug on touch screens, where a tap shows the menu for an instant or not at all.

steps.title: Fluid sizes
steps.body:
Media queries change a layout in steps, at the widths you choose. Many things look better changing smoothly instead: a heading that's a bit smaller on a phone and a bit bigger on a wide screen, or spacing that grows with the window. Sizes that do this are called **fluid**, and with a few functions they need no media queries at all.

## clamp(): a size with a floor and a ceiling

`clamp()` takes three values: the smallest it may be, the size it would like to be, and the largest it may be.

```css
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
}
```

The middle value grows with the window, since `vw`, from the CSS lessons, is a hundredth of the viewport's width. On a narrow phone it would be too small, so the floor, `1.5rem`, takes over. On a huge monitor it would be too big, so the ceiling, `3rem`, takes over. In between, it grows smoothly.

```diagram responsive-css-clamp-graph
The size stays at the floor, grows with the window, then stops at the ceiling.
```

The diagram plots this heading at the default text size. Below 320 pixels wide, the heading stays at 24 pixels. From 320 to 1280 it grows in a straight line, and from 1280 on it stays at 48. You can work those points out yourself: `1rem + 2.5vw` is 16 pixels plus a fortieth of the width, which is 24 at 320 and 48 at 1280.

Why `1rem + 2.5vw` and not just `5vw`? Because text sized only in `vw` doesn't get bigger when someone zooms in. Zooming makes CSS pixels bigger, which makes the viewport fewer CSS pixels wide, so the `vw` part shrinks by just as much and cancels the zoom out. The `rem` part grows with the zoom and with the reader's own text size setting, so they can always make the text larger. Mix in a `rem` value whenever you use `vw` for text.

`clamp()` works for spacing too, like `padding: clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem)` on a page, so a phone gets tight margins and a big screen gets generous ones.

## Keeping things from getting too wide

Long lines are hard to read: by the end of one, your eyes lose their place finding the next. About 60 to 75 characters per line reads best, and the `ch` unit, the width of a zero in the current font, measures that directly:

```css
article {
  max-inline-size: 65ch;
  margin-inline: auto;
}
```

`max-inline-size` is the logical name for `max-width`, from the previous lesson. The article fills a phone's screen, stops at about 65 characters wide on a laptop, and `margin-inline: auto` centers it.

## Pictures that fit

A picture is as wide as its file by default, so a 2000-pixel photo pokes out of a phone's screen. One rule, in nearly every stylesheet, fixes that:

```css
img {
  max-inline-size: 100%;
  block-size: auto;
}
```

The picture shrinks to fit its box, and `block-size: auto`, its height, keeps its shape instead of squashing it.

Two more properties shape pictures and videos:

- `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9` gives a box a fixed shape, so its height follows its width. It's ideal for a video frame or a placeholder that holds space before its content loads.
- `object-fit` says how a picture fills a box of a different shape. `cover` fills the box and crops what sticks out, like a photo in a frame, and `contain` fits the whole picture inside, leaving empty bands at the sides.

## Layouts that need no breakpoints

The Grid part of the previous lesson made a card grid that picks its own number of columns, with `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(15rem, 100%), 1fr))`. That's a fluid layout too: it reacts to the space it has, at every width, with no media query. Reach for fluid sizes and grids like that one first, and keep media queries for the moments a layout truly has to change shape.

examples.title: A product photo that fills its frame
examples.prompt: Every product card shows its photo in the same square frame, whatever shape the original photo is.
examples.explanation: `inline-size: 100%` makes each photo as wide as its card. `aspect-ratio: 1`, the same as `1 / 1`, makes its height equal its width, so every photo is a square, and a row of cards lines up neatly even when one photo is tall and another is wide. `object-fit: cover` fills the square and crops whatever sticks out, keeping the middle. Without it, the browser would stretch or squash each photo to fill the square. If the subject sits off-center, `object-position: top` or another position chooses which part to keep. `contain` in place of `cover` would show each whole photo instead, with empty space beside the narrow ones.

examples.title: Fluid type and spacing together
examples.prompt: A page whose headings and margins grow with the window, inside limits, with no media queries.
examples.explanation: `--space` is a custom property, from the CSS lessons, holding one fluid size that the page reuses for its padding and the space under the heading, so everything grows together. On a phone it's 1rem, on a wide screen 2.5rem, and in between it follows the window. The heading has its own `clamp()`, with a tighter `line-height` that suits big text. `margin-block-end` is the bottom margin, in logical terms. The article stops at 65 characters wide. Drag the window from narrow to wide and every one of these grows smoothly, where media queries would make them jump at each breakpoint.

steps.title: Container queries

examples.title: A card that adapts to its slot
examples.prompt: The card's container is the list item it sits in. In a slot at least 28rem wide, the picture moves beside the text.
examples.code:
• Lake Loop

    An easy walk around the water, 5 km.
examples.explanation: Each `li` is a container, and the card inside it is the element the query styles, which is why the container is the wrapper and not the card. By default the card is a one-column grid: the picture on top, the text below. When the `li` is at least 28rem wide, the card gets two columns, a 10rem one for the picture and the rest for the text. Put this list in a narrow sidebar and every card stacks. Put it in the main column and they go side by side, with the same HTML and the same CSS. A list item is a block, so it takes its width from the list, which satisfies the rule that a container can't be sized by its content.

examples.title: A card title that grows with its slot
examples.prompt: Inside the same card, the title's size follows the container's width, with a floor and a ceiling.
examples.explanation: `2cqi` is two hundredths of the container's width, so in a 20rem slot it adds 0.4rem, and in a 40rem slot it adds 0.8rem. The `1rem` keeps the size following the reader's text setting, the same reason the fluid type in the previous part mixed `rem` with `vw`. `clamp()` keeps the title between 1.125rem and 1.75rem, wherever the card goes. With `vw` in place of `cqi`, a card in the narrow sidebar would get a title as big as one in the wide column, since the window is the same width for both. If no container is found above the element, `cqi` falls back to measuring the viewport, so it never breaks.

steps.title: Themes and user preferences

examples.title: A theme built on light-dark()
examples.prompt: Every color is a token that holds a light value and a dark value. The page follows the device, unless data-theme on the html element says otherwise.
examples.explanation: `color-scheme: light dark` says the page supports both, so with no attribute set, the browser follows the device: light mode gets the first color in each `light-dark()`, dark mode the second. Add `data-theme="dark"` to the `html` element and `color-scheme` becomes `dark` alone, so every token picks its dark value, even on a device in light mode, and the browser's form fields and scrollbars turn dark too. `data-theme="light"` does the opposite. The rest of the stylesheet only ever uses the tokens, like `var(--color-accent)` for links, so it never needs to know which theme is on. The `surface` token is for cards and panels that sit a little apart from the background.

examples.title: Borders that show up in forced colors
examples.prompt: A button styled with only a background color, made usable in a Windows contrast theme.
examples.explanation: The button looks like a colored shape, and its border is transparent, so it's invisible in normal colors. In a contrast theme, the browser removes the background, and without a border the button would become plain text that nobody would recognize as a button. With a border, the browser draws it in one of the person's own colors, so the button keeps its shape. Inside the media query, `Highlight` is the system color the person chose for selected things, which makes a clear focus ring around the button when it's reached with the keyboard. `:focus-visible`, from the CSS lessons, matches when focus should be shown.

steps.title: Web fonts

examples.title: Two weights from one variable font
examples.prompt: A site's own font file, declared once and used for both its body text and its headings.
examples.explanation: One `@font-face` declares a variable font that covers every weight from 100 to 900, so the body's 400 and the headings' 720 both come from the same file, one download. A weight like 720 doesn't exist in fonts that come one file per weight, where you'd pick 700 and get the bold file. `font-display: swap` shows the text in `system-ui` straight away and swaps Inter in when it lands. Put the font in the site's own folder, at `fonts/inter-var.woff2` from the root, and the path in `url()` finds it. A preload link for the same file in each page's head would start its download sooner.

examples.title: Following the system, with no download
examples.prompt: A font setup that uses each device's own interface font for text and its own monospaced font for code.
examples.explanation: `system-ui` is the font each device uses for its own interface, so a Mac reader sees San Francisco and a Windows reader sees Segoe UI, and nobody downloads anything. `sans-serif` at the end is the last resort, in case a very old browser doesn't know `system-ui`. Code gets the same treatment: `ui-monospace` is the device's own font where every letter is the same width, the kind code needs, and Menlo and Consolas are the usual ones on Mac and Windows when that name isn't understood. `monospace` is again the last resort. A setup like this costs nothing to load, and the text is never invisible or late.

steps.title: Transitions and animations

examples.title: A card that lifts on hover
examples.prompt: A card rises a little and grows a shadow when you point at it, using only transform and a cheap shadow change.
examples.explanation: On hover, the card moves up 4 pixels with `translateY`, which only the compositing step has to handle, so it stays smooth even on a slow phone. The shadow grows at the same time. `rgb(0 0 0 / 0.15)` is black at 15 percent, so it's soft. For people who asked for less motion, the second block keeps the shadow and drops the movement: the card still shows it's under the pointer, without lifting. Using `margin-top: -4px` instead of `transform` would look the same, but it changes layout, so every frame the browser would lay out the cards below again, and on a page full of cards that's where the stutter comes from.

examples.title: A loading spinner
examples.prompt: A spinning ring made of one element, which keeps turning until the content it waits for arrives.
examples.explanation: The `div` is a circle, since `border-radius: 50%` rounds a square fully, with a gray border whose top side, `border-block-start-color`, is the accent color. The animation rotates it one full turn, `1turn`, every 800 milliseconds, forever, at an even speed thanks to `linear` easing. A `@keyframes` with only `to` starts from the element's current value. Rotating is a `transform`, so it's cheap and smooth. `role="status"` and `aria-label` tell screen readers that something is loading, since they can't see a spinning ring. Spinning in place is small, steady motion, so many sites leave spinners running even with reduced motion, slowed down rather than stopped.

recap:
- The viewport meta tag makes a phone report its real width, measured in CSS pixels, not the screen's dots.
- Media queries apply rules at the widths you choose: write mobile first, and pick breakpoints where your content needs them.
- clamp() makes fluid sizes with a floor and a ceiling, and mixing rem with vw keeps text zoomable.
- Container queries let a reused component adapt to its slot instead of the window.
- Themes are tokens in custom properties: prefers-color-scheme, color-scheme, and light-dark() give you dark mode, and a data attribute lets people choose.
- Web fonts need font-display, a fallback stack, and sometimes a preload, and system-ui needs no download at all.
- Animate transform and opacity, keep motion inside a reduced-motion check, and add view transitions as an extra.
